<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Alma S. Adams, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Summer L. Lee>: INTRODUCTION
The Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA) within the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL or the Department) protects workers' hard-earned health and retirement benefits. EBSA has many laws within its purview, including the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA),\1\ the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA),\2\ the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA),\3\ the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA),\4\ and the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA).\5\ Recently, additional requirements have been placed on the agency through the Setting Every Community Up for Retirement Enhancement (SECURE) Act,\6\ the Securing a Strong Retirement Act (SECURE 2.0),\7\ the No Surprises Act,\8\ and the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA).\9\ EBSA also has interpretive and regulatory responsibilities with respect to Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) as well as audit and oversight responsibilities with respect to the federal Thrift Savings Plan (TSP).\10\

\10\This responsibility is the result of the enactment of the Federal Employees' Retirement System Act, 5 U.S.C. Sec. 8477(g)(1). The TSP is the largest defined-contribution (DC) retirement plan in the United States, with nearly 6.85 million participants and more than $814 billion in assets according to EBSA (as of July 31, 2023). See, U.S. Dep't of Lab., Off. of Inspector Gen., Top Management and Performance Challenges Facing the U.S. Department of Labor (Nov. 2023), https:// www.oig.dol.gov/public/ DOL%202023%20Top%20Management%20and%20Performance %20Challenges.pdf.
H.R. 2869, the EBSA Investigations Transparency Act, requires the Department to produce an annual report primarily focused on the duration of EBSA's investigations. This one-sided report would not provide a complete picture of the agency's enforcement activities. Furthermore, the bill does not authorize any additional funding for EBSA, despite its critical mission and growing responsibilities. While EBSA's investigations can be lengthy, they also involve complex legal issues. Committee Democrats agree that investigations should proceed as quickly as possible while still maintaining accuracy and effectiveness, but the best way to guarantee timely investigations would be to ensure EBSA has the funding, resources, and personnel necessary to fulfill its vital mission. Unfortunately, H.R. 2869 fails to do that, representing a missed opportunity to strengthen EBSA and its enforcement capabilities.
H.R. 2869 REQUIRES A ONE-SIDED REPORT, FAILING TO ACCOUNT FOR
THE BENEFITS AND COMPLEXITY OF EBSA'S INVESTIGATIONS
The statutory purpose of ERISA is to protect the interests of participants and beneficiaries in employee benefit plans.\11\ Under ERISA, the Department has broad authority to conduct investigations; require the submission of reports, books, and records; inspect books and records; and question individuals ``in order to determine whether any person has violated or is about to violate any provision of [title I of ERISA].''\12\ Through the authority provided to the Department under ERISA, EBSA oversees approximately 801,000 private retirement plans, 2.6 million health plans, and other plans, collectively covering 156 million people and holding $14 trillion in assets.\13\ EBSA's investigations and enforcement-related efforts seek to remedy violations of the law that harm workers and their families. For example, enforcement efforts address improper denial of health insurance claims that can lead to reprocessing of claims; enforcement can also result in the recovery of retirement savings to which retirees are entitled. In Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 alone, EBSA's investigations and enforcement-related efforts led to the recovery of nearly $1.4 billion in direct payment to plans, participants, and beneficiaries.\14\ These recoveries have put money back in the pockets of America's workers and retirees.

\12\29 U.S.C. Sec. 1134(a).
\13\U.S. Dep't of Lab., Employee Benefits Security Administration, Agency Enforcement Results Archive (2024), https://www.dol.gov/ agencies/ebsa/about-ebsa/our-activities/resource-center/fact-sheets/ ebsa-monetary-results-archive.

Despite ERISA's emphasis on protecting workers' hard-earned benefits and EBSA's role in enforcing the law, Committee Republicans have recently focused solely on the duration of EBSA's investigations through oversight activities, portraying EBSA investigations as excessively long and onerous for employers.\15\ In response to oversight inquiries from Committee Republicans over the last few years, the Department provided performance metrics on EBSA's enforcement program\16\ and explained that ``[i]nvestigations--especially large and complex cases--can take time to complete, particularly in the context of EBSA's exigent resource constraints . . . The length of investigations varies with the case's size and complexity, the number of witnesses, the volume of documentary evidence, the discovery of new or unexpected evidence, changes in the law, parties' levels of cooperation and timeliness in responses to EBSA's requests, and a wide variety of other factors.''\17\ The Department also noted in response to oversight inquiries that--as of the time of their correspondence in November of 2023--only 3 percent of its civil cases open for more than 48 months were in a state of ongoing investigation.\18\
\15\Letter from Representative Virginia Foxx and Representative Bob Good to Acting Secretary of Labor Julie A. Su (Sept. 19, 2023), https:/ /edworkforce.house.gov/uploadedfiles/ 09.19.23_letter_to_dol_re_ebsa_investigations.pdf.
\16\U.S. Dep't of Lab., EBSA's Timeliness Performance Measures/ Performance Standards (Feb. 7, 2025) (on file with Committee staff).
\17\Letter from Dep't of Lab. Assistant Secretary Liz Watson to Representative Virginia Foxx and Representative Bob Good (Nov. 27, 2023) (on file with Committee staff).
\18\Id. As of November 7, 2023, EBSA had 2,297 open cases. Of these, 1,735 were civil and 562 were criminal. In total, 249 civil cases (approximately 14% of the agency's total civil cases) were listed in the agency's system as open for more than 48 months. However, only 53 of these cases (approximately 3% of the agency's total civil cases) were ongoing investigations. The other 196 cases were either referred to the Solicitor's Office; in litigation; or in the agency's voluntary compliance process, in which the investigation has been concluded and the agency is either verifying that the parties have corrected a violation or discussing correction with the parties.
Despite this, Rep. Lisa McClain (R-MI) introduced H.R. 2869, the EBSA Investigations Transparency Act on April 10, 2025. The bill would require the Department to provide an annual report to Congress regarding the status of cases in enforcement status, including active investigations or cases in which the Department ``asserted investigative authority or engaged in targeted compliance monitoring'' in the previous fiscal year. Several items that must be included in the report are specified in the bill, including the field office that opened each investigation and the date it was opened; the date documents were first requested from an entity being investigated; and whether the investigation had concluded within a 36-month period and, if not, information as to why not and an estimated date of conclusion. The bill focuses primarily on one issue in a vacuum--the duration of investigations. This could potentially discourage the Department from pursuing complex cases that are likely to yield the most significant impact for workers and their families--a strategy the Government Accountability Office has noted is an effort to maximize the Departments' limited resources.\19\ EBSA should not be under congressional pressure to prematurely close cases before documents have been obtained or violations properly investigated. Moreover, there is no information required in the report that would acknowledge any of the benefits of EBSA's enforcement, such as the amount of benefits recovered, the amount of resources spent in relation to the amount of benefits recovered, or the number of lives saved by EBSA's work through activities that result in participants' ability to access live-saving health benefits.\20\
\19\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-24-105667, Employee Benefits Security Administration: Systematic Process Needed to Better Manage Priorities and Increased Responsibilities 7 (Oct. 24, 2023), https://www.gao.gov/assets/d24105667.pdf (``EBSA prioritizes major cases to maximize limited resources. Major cases can result in greater monetary results per investigative staff day, but take longer and can be more resource-intensive.'').
\20\Timely access to health benefits can be a matter of life and death. See ERISA's 50th Anniversary: The Path To Higher Quality, Lower Cost Health Care: Hearing Before the Subcomm. on Health, Emp't, Lab., and Pensions of the H. Comm. on Educ. & the Workforce, 118th Cong. 6
(2024) (statement of Karen L. Handorf, Senior Counsel, Berger Montague).
REPUBLICANS PREVIOUSLY REPEALED CERTAIN DOL REPORTING REQUIREMENTS, BUT CONGRESS IS STILL PROVIDED ANNUAL DATA ON EBSA'S ENFORCEMENT
When ERISA was initially enacted, it required the Department to submit an annual report to Congress on its administration of title I of ERISA, describing, among other things ``the status of cases in enforcement status.''\21\ During the Republican's control of Congress in the 1990s, this provision was nullified by the Federal Reports Elimination and Sunset Act of 1995.\22\ Despite no longer being subject to this requirement, the Department has provided substantial transparency regarding EBSA's enforcement activities through an annual ``Agency Enforcement Results'' document\23\ and the Department's annual report to Congress on the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act, with which EBSA is responsible for enforcing compliance.\24\ While the Department also typically provides detailed information on EBSA's enforcement and participant assistance metrics in its annual Budget Justification,\25\ this was omitted by the Trump Administration in its FY 2026 Budget request.\26\
